title: Paul’s First Missionary Journey
overview: Acts 13 details the commissioning and initial missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas from the church at Antioch. The chapter highlights the guidance of the Holy Spirit in sending these men to preach the gospel, their encounter with opposition and spiritual conflict, and Paul’s powerful sermon in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch. This chapter marks a pivotal moment in the spread of Christianity beyond Jewish communities to the Gentiles, emphasizing God’s faithfulness to His promises through Jesus Christ. It showcases the early church’s mission strategy, the role of the Holy Spirit, and the challenges faced in proclaiming salvation to both Jews and Gentiles.
structure:
**Verses 1-3: The Commissioning at Antioch.** The church at Antioch, led by prophets and teachers, fasts and prays as the Holy Spirit directs them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for missionary work. This divine commissioning underscores the Spirit’s active role in mission.

**Verses 4-12: Ministry in Cyprus and Confrontation with Elymas.** Paul and Barnabas travel to Cyprus, preaching in synagogues and encountering Elymas, a sorcerer opposing their message. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, rebukes Elymas and causes temporary blindness, leading the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus to believe.

**Verses 13-41: Paul’s Sermon in Pisidian Antioch.** Paul delivers a comprehensive sermon recounting Israel’s history, God’s promises, and the fulfillment in Jesus Christ’s resurrection. He calls his listeners to repentance and faith, highlighting forgiveness of sins and justification through Christ.

**Verses 42-52: Response and Opposition.** Gentiles eagerly receive the gospel, but Jewish opposition intensifies, resulting in persecution and expulsion of Paul and Barnabas. Despite this, the disciples rejoice and are filled with the Holy Spirit, demonstrating perseverance and joy in suffering.

keyVerses.text: As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the divine initiative and guidance of the Holy Spirit in mission work, emphasizing that gospel ministry is a calling from God, not merely human decision.

keyVerses.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?
keyVerses.significance: Paul’s confrontation with Elymas demonstrates the spiritual battle underlying gospel ministry and the authority given by the Holy Spirit to oppose falsehood and opposition to God’s truth.

keyVerses.text: Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins:
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the core message of the gospel preached by Paul—through Jesus Christ, forgiveness of sins is offered, fulfilling God’s redemptive plan.

keyVerses.text: For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.
keyVerses.significance: Paul and Barnabas affirm their mission to the Gentiles, fulfilling God’s promise to extend salvation beyond Israel, marking a major expansion in the early church’s outreach.

characters.name: Paul (Saul)
characters.description: Originally known as Saul, Paul is a key apostle chosen and empowered by the Holy Spirit to preach the gospel. In this chapter, he boldly confronts opposition and delivers a foundational sermon on Jesus as the promised Savior.

characters.name: Barnabas
characters.description: A respected prophet and teacher in the Antioch church, Barnabas partners with Paul in the missionary journey, supporting and encouraging the spread of the gospel.

characters.name: Elymas (Barjesus)
characters.description: A Jewish sorcerer and false prophet who opposes Paul and Barnabas’s message, attempting to turn the Roman proconsul away from the faith. His temporary blindness signifies divine judgment against spiritual opposition.

characters.name: Sergius Paulus
characters.description: The Roman deputy (proconsul) of Cyprus, described as prudent, who responds positively to Paul’s message after witnessing the judgment on Elymas, illustrating the gospel’s power to convert influential leaders.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes the Holy Spirit’s role in directing and commissioning missionaries, showing that gospel work is initiated and empowered by God’s sovereign will.
The confrontation with Elymas highlights the reality of spiritual opposition to the gospel, reminding believers of the ongoing battle between truth and falsehood.
Paul’s sermon traces God’s faithfulness from Israel’s history to the resurrection of Jesus, affirming that Christ is the promised Savior who brings forgiveness and justification.
The chapter marks a significant expansion of the gospel mission to Gentiles, fulfilling Old Testament prophecies and God’s plan for salvation to reach all nations.
Despite opposition and expulsion, the disciples rejoice and remain filled with the Holy Spirit, modeling faithful endurance in the face of trials.

historicalContext: This chapter takes place in the early first century AD, during the Roman Empire’s rule over the eastern Mediterranean. Antioch, a major city in Syria, was a diverse cultural and religious center where the early church flourished. Cyprus and Pisidian Antioch were key locations on trade routes, facilitating the spread of ideas and the gospel. The presence of synagogues indicates a significant Jewish diaspora population, providing initial platforms for Paul and Barnabas’s preaching. The political context includes Roman provincial governance, exemplified by Sergius Paulus, who held authority in Cyprus. The chapter reflects the early church’s transition from a primarily Jewish movement to a mission embracing Gentiles, navigating cultural and religious tensions.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign election and the Spirit’s role in calling and empowering missionaries. Paul’s sermon is seen as a clear proclamation of justification by faith alone through Christ’s resurrection, fulfilling Old Testament promises.

Dispensationalists highlight the distinct phases of God’s redemptive plan, noting the transition from Israel to the church age. The mission to the Gentiles is viewed as a new dispensation, with Paul’s ministry inaugurating this era.

Early church fathers often interpreted Paul’s sermon typologically, seeing Israel’s history as a foreshadowing of Christ’s work. They stressed the importance of the Spirit’s power in overcoming opposition and spreading the gospel.

crossReferences.connection: God’s command to be a light to the Gentiles is rooted in this prophecy, which Paul cites in Acts 13:47 to justify the mission to the Gentiles.
Quoted in Acts 13:33, this verse affirms Jesus as God’s Son, underscoring the resurrection as fulfillment of Messianic prophecy.
Paul’s teaching on justification by faith apart from the law in Romans echoes the message of forgiveness and justification proclaimed in Acts 13.
John the Baptist’s testimony about Jesus as the Lamb of God (John 1:29) parallels John’s role in preparing the way mentioned in Acts 13:24-25.
Paul’s experience of opposition and reliance on God’s strength in weakness relates to the spiritual conflict and perseverance seen in Acts 13.

application: Seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit in all ministry and decision-making, trusting God’s sovereign calling.
Stand firm against spiritual opposition, relying on God’s power to overcome falsehood and opposition.
Proclaim the gospel boldly, emphasizing forgiveness of sins and justification through Jesus Christ alone.
Embrace the mission to reach all people, including those outside our cultural or religious background.
Rejoice and remain faithful in the face of persecution, knowing the Holy Spirit empowers believers.
Use biblical history and prophecy to strengthen faith and understanding of God’s redemptive plan.
conclusion: Acts 13 stands as a foundational chapter in the book of Acts, marking the birth of the church’s missionary outreach under the Spirit’s direction. It reveals the power of the gospel to confront spiritual darkness, the faithfulness of God in fulfilling His promises through Christ, and the expansion of salvation to the Gentiles. For believers today, it challenges us to be Spirit-led, courageous in proclamation, and joyful in suffering, trusting that God’s purposes will prevail through the spread of His word.
timeline: c. AD 46-48 - Paul and Barnabas’ First Missionary Journey

definitions.definition: Another term for the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity who empowers, guides, and sanctifies believers.
To set apart or designate for a special purpose, especially in a spiritual or ministerial context.
A Roman official governing a province, with administrative and judicial authority, such as Sergius Paulus in Cyprus.
In this context, the decay or decomposition of a dead body; used metaphorically for death and decay that Christ did not undergo.
Cunning or craftiness, often with a negative connotation of deceit or trickery.

outline.heading: Commissioning of Paul and Barnabas
outline.description: The church at Antioch, led by prophets and teachers, fasts and prays as the Holy Spirit directs them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special missionary task.

outline.heading: Ministry and Confrontation in Cyprus
outline.description: Paul and Barnabas preach in Jewish synagogues and confront Elymas the sorcerer, resulting in his temporary blindness and the conversion of the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus.

outline.heading: Paul’s Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
outline.description: Paul delivers a detailed sermon recounting Israel’s history, God’s promises, and the resurrection of Jesus as the fulfillment, calling listeners to repentance and faith.

outline.heading: Response and Opposition
outline.description: Gentiles eagerly receive the gospel while Jewish opposition grows, leading to persecution and expulsion of Paul and Barnabas, who respond with joy and reliance on the Holy Spirit.
